cells.tense: You are right here, feeling with someone and still holding the shape of your own life whole.
cells.ask: Make one structure out of something you felt with someone this week — a rule, a plan, a habit you both keep — and let it stand whether they join in or not.
cells.core:
You feel what's going on with people, and it doesn't pull you out of yourself. That's the rare part. You can sit across from someone who's having a hard time and stay with them and stay with your own read of the room — you don't flood, and you don't step back.

You're also the one deciding how things get arranged. What gets written down, what gets repeated, what people can count on. Being able to feel what someone's carrying tells you what the arrangement should hold. You stay under the weight when something leans on you, when the plan changes, when it runs long — steady, without forcing — and that's what keeps it standing after today. It costs you the ordinary tiredness of staying.
cells.sheetLine: You feel with people and still hold the frame. That's the balance.

cells.tense: You will keep building the structure around someone else's moods, and you are already bracing for the next one that isn't yours.
cells.ask: Write down the one arrangement you made for someone else's feelings and set a date this week when you stop holding it. Tell them it's done.
cells.core:
You can feel what someone else is feeling before they show it, and your instinct is to build something around it — a rule, a routine, a way of phrasing things so they don't have to say it. You're already arranging the room for a mood that hasn't arrived.

The building is real and it holds. That's not the problem. The problem is you can't tell whose mood you're bracing for anymore. You move a piece of your own day to make room for something that isn't there yet, and the arrangement starts deciding instead of you.

One ending, honored rather than resented, is what this needs. Not a big reckoning. Just one thing you stop holding up, and the room gets lighter.

cells.tense: You used to be in the room with people, and now the structure stands without you in it.
cells.ask: Pick one person you'd normally keep at arm's length and adjust something small — a shorter reply, one honest sentence about your day. Then notice how it lands, not how it felt to send.
cells.core:
The structure is there. You keep things running, you know who needs what, you're the one people call when the plan falls apart — and none of that requires you to be in the room with them. The relationship stays at the surface and it works, so nothing forced the issue.

The work isn't to manufacture feeling. It's tuning: sensing the moment to lean in, the moment to let it be. That skill is still yours, it's just out of tune right now. It returns through small adjustments, not big declarations.

Start with one person and one small change. A little more contact than habit allows, then read the difference it makes in the other person's face.

cells.tense: You are already holding people steady, and you are calling it just doing the job.
cells.ask: Say one true sentence out loud about how you actually feel toward someone you've been steadying this week, and write it down under a heading you wouldn't choose.
cells.core:
You're already feeling with people. It's in how you set things up, what you anticipate, the way the structure bends to hold someone before they ask. You'd describe all of it as being organized, or practical, or just handling it. That's the disguise.

Underneath is real recognition — feeling with someone rather than just about them. It's running. It's shaping the room. It's just not something you name as yours.

Seeing the pattern for what it is doesn't require feeling more. It's a matter of noticing the mechanism — the way care shows up as arrangement. Once you see that, it gets harder to call logistics.
cells.sheetLine: The care is already running. You're calling it logistics.
